title: Our basic needs: why we need air, water, food, clothes and a home every day

summary.text: You breathe about 20 times a minute, and you cannot stop for long. Every person needs air, water and food to stay alive, and clothes and a home to stay safe and well. These five are our basic needs. We need them again and again because the body keeps using them up: every breath carries used air out, and your skin lets water out even when you feel dry. Toys, phones and sweets are wants. They are nice to have, but we can live without them.
summary.art: A child sitting on a balcony of a city flat, breathing in, holding a steel tumbler of water, with a plate of idli beside them, a cotton shirt on, and the walls and roof of the home around them, each of the five needs gently labelled.

intro.hook: Sit down and take a normal breath. Now hold it and count slowly. Stop as soon as you want to. Soon your body makes you breathe again. You can save a snack for later. Why can't you save up a breath?
intro.text: Your body uses air every few seconds, water every few hours and food a few times a day. In this unit you find out why. You test whether your dry hand is giving out water. You find out whether a ring of water can keep hungry ants away from sugar. You sort needs from wants, and argue about the hard ones. And you learn the simple ways families in India keep air, water, food, clothes and homes clean and safe.
intro.art: A girl sitting cross-legged on a mat, cheeks puffed, holding her breath, with a clock on the wall behind her and her mother counting on her fingers.

outcomes: I can name the five basic needs, and say which three we cannot live without at all, and why.
I can explain that my body keeps using up air and water, and show with my own test that my skin gives out water even when I feel dry.
I can say what happens to air when I breathe: I take in oxygen, and I breathe out carbon dioxide and water.
I can say why clothes and a home are needs, and what each one protects us from.
I can give ways to keep each need clean and safe: fresh air, clean covered water, covered food, clean dry clothes and a clean, airy home.
I can tell a need from a want, and explain why something can be a need in one place and a want in another.
I can tell how Santorio weighed himself for years and found that the body loses water we cannot see.

terms.meaning: The things every person must have to live and stay well: air, water, food, clothes and a home.
terms.example: A baby, a grandmother and a cricketer all have the same five basic needs.
terms.art: Five simple pictures in a row: a breeze, a tumbler of water, a plate of rice, a shirt and a house.

terms.meaning: Something we cannot live without, or cannot stay healthy without.
terms.example: Drinking water is a need. Without it, a person becomes very ill within a day or two in hot weather.
terms.art: A child drinking from a steel tumbler on a hot day.

terms.meaning: Something nice to have that we can live without.
terms.example: A new cricket bat is a want. You can stay alive and healthy without it.
terms.art: A shiny new cricket bat in a shop window.

terms.meaning: A gas in the air that every cell in your body needs. About one-fifth of the air is oxygen.
terms.example: When you breathe in, your lungs take oxygen out of the air and pass it into your blood.
terms.art: Air going into a child's nose, with tiny dots marked O for oxygen.

terms.meaning: A gas your cells make as they use food for energy. You breathe it out.
terms.example: The air you breathe out has about 100 times as much carbon dioxide as the air you breathe in.
terms.art: Air coming out of a child's mouth, with tiny dots marked CO2.

terms.meaning: Two soft, spongy organs in your chest. They fill with air when you breathe in.
terms.example: Put your hands on your ribs and breathe in deeply. Your ribs move out as your lungs fill.
terms.art: A child with hands on their ribs, and a simple drawing of two lungs inside the chest.

terms.meaning: What your body needs to move, grow, think and keep warm. It comes from food.
terms.example: After a long game of kho-kho, you feel hungry, because your body has used energy.
terms.art: Children running in a game of kho-kho in a building courtyard.

terms.meaning: Water that leaves your skin all the time without you noticing. Insensible means you cannot sense it.
terms.example: In the Hidden Water Test, a plastic bag on a dry hand turned misty inside within minutes.
terms.art: A hand inside a clear plastic bag, with tiny drops on the inside of the plastic.

terms.meaning: When the body has lost more water than it has taken in. It can cause a headache, tiredness and dark yellow urine.
terms.example: A child who plays in the May sun and forgets to drink may get a headache from dehydration.
terms.art: A tired child in the shade on a hot day, with a water bottle being handed to them.

terms.meaning: Water that is clean enough to drink without making you ill. Another name for it is potable water.
terms.example: Boiled water that has cooled in a covered steel pot is safe drinking water.
terms.art: A covered steel pot of water with a long-handled ladle hanging beside it.

terms.meaning: Water that stays still in one place for days, such as in a flower-pot plate, a cooler or an old tyre.
terms.example: Mosquitoes lay their eggs in stagnant water. The young ones grow there in about a week.
terms.art: A clay flower-pot plate on a balcony with still water in it, and tiny wrigglers swimming.

terms.meaning: Fresh air coming into a room and used air going out, through windows, doors and vents.
terms.example: A kitchen with an exhaust fan and an open window has good ventilation, so smoke and steam go out.
terms.art: A kitchen with an open window and an exhaust fan, with arrows showing air coming in and going out.

terms.meaning: A place that protects us from heat, cold, rain, wind and animals. A home is a shelter.
terms.example: In a cyclone in Chennai, families stay inside strong buildings for shelter.
terms.art: A building standing firm in heavy rain and wind, with warm lit windows.

terms.meaning: A very thin thread. Cloth is woven or knitted from fibres such as cotton, wool or polyester.
terms.example: Pull a loose thread from an old cotton towel, and you can see it is made of even thinner fibres twisted together.
terms.art: A close-up of a cotton thread untwisted into many fine fibres.

explanations.definition: Basic needs are the things every person must have to live and stay well: air, water, food, clothes and a home.
explanations.description: Three of the five keep us alive. Without air, a person can live only a few minutes. Without water, only a few days. Without food, a few weeks. The other two, clothes and a home, keep us safe and healthy. They protect us from sun, cold, rain, wind, insects and dirt. Every person on Earth has these same five needs, wherever they live and however rich or poor they are.
examples: A newborn baby needs milk, which gives both food and water, plus warm cloth and a safe home.
A soldier in the snow of Ladakh needs thick clothes and a warm shelter to stay alive.
A fisherwoman in Kochi needs drinking water on the boat, even with the sea all around her, because sea water is too salty to drink.
explanations.art: Five cards laid out on a table: a breeze, a tumbler of water, a plate of rice and dal, a cotton shirt, and a small house.
explanations.context: This card names the five basic needs and says which three keep us alive.

explanations.definition: We breathe in air for its oxygen. Our cells use oxygen to get energy from food, and they make carbon dioxide, which we breathe out.
explanations.description: Every cell in your body is using food for energy right now. To do it, each cell needs oxygen. Your lungs take oxygen from the air, and your blood carries it everywhere. The cells give back carbon dioxide, and your blood carries it to your lungs to breathe out. Your body stores very little oxygen, so you must keep breathing. That is why you could not save up a breath. A child at rest breathes about 20 times a minute.
examples: After running, you breathe faster, because your muscles are using food and oxygen faster.
Air breathed out still has some oxygen in it. That is why mouth-to-mouth breathing can help a person who has stopped breathing.
Smoke from burning rubbish or a smoky chulha fills the lungs with harmful particles, so clean air matters as much as air itself.
explanations.art: A simple body outline with air going into the lungs, red lines carrying oxygen to the arms and legs, and blue lines bringing carbon dioxide back to the lungs.
explanations.context: This card is about why you can never stop breathing for long: your cells need oxygen all the time.

explanations.concept: Why we need water, every day
explanations.definition: About 60 percent of a grown-up's body is water, and a child's body is a little more. Water carries food and oxygen in the blood, helps digest food, takes away waste and cools us as sweat.
explanations.description: Your body loses water all day. It leaves in urine, in sweat, in every breath, and through your skin even when you feel dry. You saw this in the Hidden Water Test. Even on a cool day, a grown-up loses a few glasses of water through skin and breath alone. So we must drink every day to put that water back. Food helps too: rice, fruit, curd and rasam are mostly water. Thirst is the body's signal that it needs more. Dark yellow urine is another sign.
examples: On a hot day in Madurai, a child playing outside sweats a lot and needs to drink much more than on a cool day.
Breathe on a cold steel plate, and a mist of water forms. That water came from inside you.
A slice of watermelon is mostly water, so eating it also gives you water.
explanations.art: A child drinking water, with arrows showing water leaving their body as breath, sweat from the skin and a trip to the toilet.
explanations.context: This card is about why we need to drink every day: the body keeps letting water go.

explanations.definition: Food gives the body energy to move, think and stay warm. It also gives the materials to grow and to mend cuts, bones and muscles.
explanations.description: Your cells use food for energy all the time, even while you sleep. Your heart beats, your brain thinks and your body stays at about 37 degrees Celsius, and all of that needs energy. Food also gives building materials. A child grows taller because food becomes new bone and muscle. The body can store some food as fat, so a person can live for weeks without eating. But they become weak and ill, and a growing child stops growing well.
examples: A cut on your knee heals in a week. The new skin is built from food you ate.
Ragi, rice and wheat give energy. Dal, eggs, fish and milk give materials for growing.
When you are ill and cannot eat much, you feel weak, because your body is short of energy.
explanations.art: A thali of rice, dal, a vegetable and curd, with arrows from it to a running child, a growing height chart and a healing knee.
explanations.context: This card is about the two jobs food does: giving energy and building the body.

explanations.definition: Clothes protect the skin from the sun, cold, rain, wind, insects and dirt, and help the body stay at the right temperature.
explanations.description: Your body works best at about 37 degrees Celsius. In hot weather, the body sweats, and the sweat cools it as it dries. Loose cotton clothes help, because cotton soaks up sweat and lets air move past the skin. In cold weather, wool and thick layers help, because they trap still air, and still air slows heat leaving the body. Clothes also protect the skin from sunburn, mosquito bites and cuts. Clothes must be washed and dried in the sun, or sweat and dirt let germs and mould grow.
examples: Farmers in the fields of Andhra Pradesh often wear a cotton towel on the head to keep off the sun.
In Shimla in January, people wear woollen sweaters, caps and shawls.
A full-sleeved shirt in the evening keeps mosquitoes from biting your arms.
explanations.art: Three children side by side: one in a loose cotton shirt in the sun, one in a woollen sweater and cap in snow, one in a raincoat in the rain.
explanations.context: This card is about how clothes protect us, and why different weather needs different clothes.

explanations.definition: A home, or shelter, protects us from heat, cold, rain, wind and animals, and gives a safe place to sleep, cook, store water and keep clean.
explanations.description: A good home keeps the rain out and lets fresh air and sunlight in. It needs windows on more than one side, so air can flow through. The kitchen needs a window or an exhaust fan, so smoke and steam can leave. Used water must drain away through pipes, so it does not stand around and breed mosquitoes. Rubbish goes into a covered bin and out of the house every day. Homes are built to suit their place. Houses in rainy Kerala and snowy Himachal have sloping roofs so that rain and snow slide off.
examples: A flat in Hyderabad has windows on two sides, so a breeze can blow through.
A thatched hut in a village stays cool in summer, because thick thatch slows the sun's heat.
Houses in flood areas of Assam are often built on stilts, high above the water.
explanations.art: A cut-away drawing of a city flat with arrows of air flowing in through one window and out through another, a kitchen exhaust fan and a drain pipe.
explanations.context: This card is about what a home protects us from, and what makes a home healthy.

explanations.definition: Taking care of our needs means keeping our air, water, food, clothes and home clean and safe, so that they keep us well instead of making us ill.
explanations.description: Each need can carry germs or harm if we are careless. Air: open windows, and keep smoke away from children. Water: drink only safe water, boiled or filtered, and keep it covered. Pour it out with a ladle instead of dipping a tumbler in with your hand. Empty any still water at home once a week, so mosquitoes cannot breed. Food: cover it from flies, ants and dust, and wash hands before eating. Clothes: wash them and dry them in the sun. Home: sweep, keep drains clear and put rubbish in a covered bin.
examples: A matka with a tap lets everyone take water without dipping their hands in.
Many families keep a sugar dabba standing in a plate of water, so ants cannot climb in.
Upturning flower-pot plates once a week stops mosquitoes breeding on a balcony.
explanations.art: A tidy Indian kitchen: a covered water pot with a ladle, covered dabbas, a plate of water under the sugar tin, an open window and a covered bin.
explanations.context: This card gives the simple ways families keep each basic need clean and safe.

explanations.description: A need is something we cannot live or stay well without. A want is nice to have. Many things are easy to sort: water is a need, a video game is a want. Others are hard. A sweater is a need in Shimla in winter and a want in Chennai in May. A fan is a want for a person who stays healthy without one, but in a heatwave it can protect an old person's health. People also argue about whether there are other needs, such as love, friends, learning and play. Here are two views.
examples: Medicine is a want for a healthy person, but a need for a person with diabetes who needs insulin.
A mobile phone is usually a want. For a fisherwoman checking a cyclone warning at sea, it can save her life.
A child who has food and a home but no one who cares for them does not grow up well.

perspectives.who: Abraham Maslow, a psychologist in the USA, in 1943
perspectives.explanation: People meet their needs in order. First come the body's needs, such as air, water and food. Then safety. Then love and friends. Then being respected. Only then do people work on growing into their best selves.

perspectives.who: Later researchers, including a 2011 study of people in 123 countries
perspectives.explanation: Needs do not always come in a strict order. Many people who are poor and often hungry still feel loved and respected, and these things matter to their happiness too. The needs work side by side.
Whether something is a need depends on the person and the place. The same thing can be a need for one person and a want for another.

explanations.art: A balance scale with a sweater on one side, and two small pictures beside it: snowy Shimla and sunny Chennai.
explanations.context: This card is about how to tell needs from wants, and why the line between them is argued about.

explanations.concept: Other living beings have needs too
explanations.definition: Plants and animals need air, water and food too, and many need shelter. A plant also needs light, because they make their own food from air, water and sunlight.
explanations.description: An ant colony must feed their queen and their young, so worker ants search for food all day. They come into kitchens because sugar and crumbs are easy food. A house gecko lives behind a picture frame, because the wall is a shelter and the light brings insects to eat. A tulsi plant in a pot needs water every day in summer. A crow drinks from a bowl on a balcony in May. Our homes meet the needs of many others, as well as our own.
examples: A pigeon builds a nest on the ledge of a flat, because the ledge is a shelter from rain and cats.
A money plant on a windowsill turns their leaves towards the light.
Ants carry sugar home inside their body and share it with the ants in the nest.
explanations.art: A city flat with small labels: ants on a kitchen shelf, a gecko behind a picture frame, a tulsi plant on the balcony, a crow drinking from a bowl.
explanations.context: This card is about the needs of the other living beings who share our homes.

agreed.text: Every person needs air, water and food to stay alive, and clothes and shelter to stay safe and healthy.
agreed.evidence: Doctors and scientists everywhere agree. People who go without any of these become ill, and without air, water or food they die.

agreed.text: The body loses water all day, through urine, sweat, breath and the skin, so we must drink every day.
agreed.evidence: Santorio's weighing chair in 1614, and many careful measurements since, show the body losing weight as water even when no sweat can be seen. You saw it in the Hidden Water Test.

agreed.text: We breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide, and our cells use oxygen to get energy from food.
agreed.evidence: Breathed-out air has less oxygen and much more carbon dioxide than room air. Limewater turns milky with breathed-out air, but hardly at all with room air.

agreed.text: Dirty water, uncovered food and stagnant water spread illness.
agreed.evidence: Cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea spread through dirty water and food. Dengue and malaria spread by mosquitoes, which breed in still water. Clean water and covered food have saved millions of lives.

challenging.claim: If you are not sweating, you are not losing water.
challenging.who: A very common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: You cannot see or feel any water leaving your skin on a cool day.
challenging.against: A plastic bag over a dry hand turns misty within minutes. Water leaves the skin and the breath all the time. Santorio measured it with a weighing chair 400 years ago.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that we only lose water when we can feel sweat.

challenging.claim: Everyone must drink exactly 8 glasses of water a day.
challenging.who: Common advice on posters and in magazines
challenging.for: The body does lose a lot of water every day, and drinking enough is important.
challenging.against: How much a person needs depends on their size, the weather and how active they are. Food such as rice, fruit, curd and rasam gives water too. For healthy children, drinking when thirsty and more in hot weather is a good guide.
challenging.context: This card is about a popular rule for how much water to drink.

challenging.claim: A cool room with the AC on has fresh air.
challenging.for: The air feels cool and pleasant, so it seems clean.
challenging.against: Most split ACs in homes cool the same room air again and again. They do not bring in fresh air. With the windows shut, the carbon dioxide from everyone's breath builds up. Opening a window for a while lets fresh air in.
challenging.context: This card is about whether cool air is the same as fresh air.

challenging.claim: People always meet their needs in a fixed order: food first, then safety, then love, then respect.
challenging.who: Abraham Maslow's pyramid of needs, from 1943, as it is often taught
challenging.for: A starving person thinks mostly about food. It makes sense that the body's needs come first.
challenging.against: Large surveys in many countries found that people who are poor or hungry can still feel loved and respected, and that these needs matter to them at the same time as food. Maslow himself did not draw his idea as a strict pyramid.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous idea that our needs come in a ladder, one step at a time.

challenging.claim: Ants come only to dirty homes.
challenging.for: Ants often appear where food has been spilt.
challenging.against: Ants come wherever there is food and water they can reach, even in very clean homes. One grain of sugar is enough. Their scouts search all day, because their colony needs food.
challenging.context: This card is about why ants come into our kitchens.

big_questions.q: The water you drank this morning is already leaving you through your skin and breath. Is the water inside you part of you, or just passing through?
big_questions.hint: Think about the misty bag, and where that water goes next.

big_questions.q: You can store food in your body as fat, and some water, but almost no air. Why do you think the body cannot store up air?
big_questions.hint: Think about how quickly you need oxygen, and how much space a gas takes up.

big_questions.q: Is love a basic need, like water? How could anyone find out?
big_questions.hint: Think about babies, and what happens to children who have food but no one to care for them.

big_questions.q: Ants need food just as we do. When ants come for our sugar, whose food is it?
big_questions.hint: Think about who made the sugar, who bought it, and who needs it.

big_questions.q: A sweater is a need in Shimla and a want in Chennai. Is anything a need everywhere, for everyone?
big_questions.hint: Think about air and water, and whether even they ever change.

big_questions.q: Many people in the world do not have safe drinking water. What would it take for everyone to have it?
big_questions.hint: Think about wells, pipes, filters, money, and who decides.

story.title: The Day the Water Lorry Was Late
story.note: The story is made up. The science in it is true: the body loses water through breath and skin all day, thirst can come late on a hot day, and families in many Indian cities plan their water carefully when supply is short.
text: It was May in Chennai, and the sun was already hot at eight in the morning. Meenakshi was nine. She stood on the balcony of their third-floor flat and looked down at the gate. Every Tuesday a water lorry came and filled the big tank of their building. Today it had not come.
"The pipe from the lorry company is broken," said Amma, putting down her phone. "They will come tomorrow. Until then, we have what is in our drum and the bottles in the kitchen."
Meenakshi looked at the blue drum in the bathroom. It was half full. Her little brother Arjun, who was six, looked at it too.
"That's lots," he said. "I can still have my bucket bath and play with the hose on the balcony."
Amma laughed, but only a little. "Let us make a plan first. Meenakshi, get a paper."
They sat on the floor of the hall under the fan. Amma drew a line down the middle of the paper. On one side she wrote NEED. On the other side she wrote WANT.
"What do we need water for today?" she asked. "Things we cannot do without."
"Drinking," said Meenakshi at once.
"Cooking rice and sambar," said Paati from her chair.
"Washing hands before we eat, and after the toilet," said Meenakshi. "Or germs get on our food."
"Flushing the toilet," added Arjun, and everyone laughed, because it was true.
"And the wants?" asked Amma.
Arjun thought hard. "Playing with the hose," he said sadly. "Washing the car. A long bath."
"What about the tulsi plant?" asked Meenakshi. "Is that a need or a want?"
"For us, maybe a want," said Paati. "For the tulsi, a need. She has no drum of her own."
They decided to give the tulsi the water left over from washing the rice. It had a little starch in it, but it was clean enough for a plant.
Amma filled four steel bottles with boiled drinking water, one for each of them, and put them on the dining table. "This is drinking water only," she said. "Drink from it all day."
By eleven o'clock, the flat was hot. Arjun had been building a fort of cushions and jumping off the sofa. His bottle was still full.
"Arjun, drink some water," said Meenakshi.
"I'm not thirsty," he said. "I haven't sweated at all. Look, my arms are dry. So I haven't lost any water."

Meenakshi frowned. Last week, in her homeschool science, she had put a clear plastic bag over her own dry hand. In a few minutes, the inside had turned misty. Then little drops had formed on the plastic. Her hand had been giving out water the whole time, and she had not felt it.
"Come here," she said. "Breathe on this." She held up a cold steel plate from the fridge. Arjun huffed on it. A grey mist spread over the steel and slowly faded.

"That's water," said Meenakshi. "From inside you. Every breath takes a little water out. And your skin lets water out all the time, even when it feels dry. Your body is like our drum with a tiny leak. You have to keep filling it up."
Arjun looked at the plate, then at his bottle. He drank half of it in one go.
At two o'clock, Paati said her head was aching. Meenakshi noticed that Paati's bottle was nearly full too. Paati often forgot to drink, because she did not feel thirsty.
"Paati," said Meenakshi, "older people sometimes don't feel thirsty even when their body needs water. My science card said so. Please drink."
Paati raised her eyebrows. "Who is teaching whom today?" But she drank a full tumbler, and then another, slowly. By evening her headache had gone.
That night Amma looked at the drum. There was still a little water at the bottom. "We did it," she said. "Because we knew what was a need and what was a want."
Arjun was looking out of the balcony door. On the railing sat a crow, panting, with her beak open in the heat.
"Amma," he said. "The crow needs water too. Can we give her some?"
Amma smiled and filled a small clay bowl from the kitchen. Arjun put it on the balcony floor. The crow hopped down, looked at him with one eye, and drank.

The next morning, the water lorry came roaring through the gate at six o'clock. Arjun ran to the balcony to watch the long pipe fill the tank. Then he went straight to the dining table and drank a tumbler of water before anyone asked.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Arjun thought that a dry body is not losing water. Meenakshi knew from her own test that skin and breath let water out all the time, so the body needs topping up even without sweat. Paati shows a true fact: older people often feel less thirsty, so they can become dehydrated without noticing. Sorting needs from wants is how the family made a small amount of water last.
ask: Arjun said he had not lost any water because his arms were dry. What did Meenakshi show him?
Which things did the family put on the NEED side? Which went on the WANT side?
Paati said the water was a want for the family but a need for the tulsi. What did she mean?
Why did Paati get a headache, and what made it go away?
If your family had only one drum of water for a day, what would you use it for first?

games.title: Pack the Boat: a needs-and-wants card game
games.context: This is a card game. Each player packs a small boat for a three-day trip to an island. You can pack only 8 cards. Then the weather cards show whether you packed what you need.

printables.title: 24 packing cards to cut out
items: Teddy bear (want, but it may comfort you)

printables.title: 8 weather and event cards
items: Hot sun all day. Did you pack water? If not, lose 2 points.
Heavy rain at night. Did you pack shelter? If not, lose 2 points.
A cold wind. Did you pack a shawl or tent? If not, lose 1 point.
Mosquitoes at dusk. Did you pack a net or long sleeves? If not, lose 1 point.
The well water is muddy. Did you pack a filter or enough water? If not, lose 2 points.
You are hungry. Did you pack food? If not, lose 2 points.
You cut your foot. Did you pack a first-aid box? If not, lose 1 point.
A quiet evening. If you packed a want card, gain 1 point for fun.

setup.art: Twenty-four packing cards laid face up on a floor, with pictures of water bottles, rice, a tent, a phone and chocolates.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the packing cards. Each player picks 8.

setup.art: An event card reading 'Heavy rain at night' turned over, and two players checking their 8 cards for a tent or plastic sheet.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over an event card. Did you pack what you need?

rules: Lay all 24 packing cards face up.
Each player picks 8 cards for their boat. Two players may pick the same thing, so write it on your score sheet instead of taking the card.
Shuffle the event cards. Turn them over one by one and read each aloud.
Each player checks their 8 cards and changes their points.
After all 8 events, the player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: try to finish with 10 points or more.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Lay the packing cards face up. 3. Explain the trip.
flow.say: We are going to an island for three days. There's no shop and no house. You can pack only 8 things. Choose carefully.
flow.kid: You are going to an island. You can pack 8 things. Choose!
flow.context: This is the first step of Pack the Boat, a game about needs and wants.

flow.do: Each player picks 8 cards and says why they chose each one.
flow.say: Pick your 8. Tell me why you chose each one. Is it a need or a want?
flow.kid: Pick 8 cards. Say why for each one.

flow.do: Turn over the event cards one at a time. Each player checks their boat and changes their points.
flow.say: Here comes the weather. Hot sun all day. Who packed water?
flow.kid: Turn over an event card. Did you pack what you need?

flow.do: Add up the points and talk about it.
flow.say: Who did best? What would you pack differently next time? Was any want card useful?
flow.kid: Add up your points. What would you change next time?
flow.think: The teddy bear is a want. Could comfort ever be a need?

experiments.title: The Hidden Water Test: does a dry hand give out water?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put a clear plastic bag over your dry hand, and another over an empty tumbler, and watch what happens inside each one.
experiments.question: Your hand feels dry. Does it still give out water? If mist appears in the bag, where does it come from?
experiments.predict: One bag goes over your dry hand. Another goes over an empty steel tumbler. What will the inside of each bag look like after 15 minutes? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two bags of the same kind, clean and dry inside. Both stay in the same room, away from the fan and the sun, for the same 15 minutes. Only one thing is different: one bag holds your hand and one holds an empty tumbler. The tumbler bag shows whether the mist could come from the room's air.
results_table: Bag on my hand: what I see and feel
Bag on the tumbler: what I see

materials.item: two clean, clear plastic bags, such as zip bags or the bags bread comes in. They must be see-through.
two loose rubber bands or hair bands, or two pieces of string
a dry steel tumbler
a clock, or a phone timer
a dry towel, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Plastic bags are only for hands and tumblers. Never put one over the head or face. Keep the band loose, so it does not squeeze the wrist. Take the bag off at once if the hand feels uncomfortable. A grown-up stays near.

schedule.what: Guess, then put one bag over a dry hand and one over a tumbler. Watch for 15 minutes. Compare and explain.

experiments.record: Fill in the table at 0, 5, 10 and 15 minutes. Then draw both bags as they looked at the end, with any drops you saw.

setup.art: A child drying their hands on a towel, with two clear plastic bags, two hair bands and a steel tumbler on the table.
setup.caption: 1. Dry your hands well. Wait two minutes.

setup.art: A child sitting at a table with one hand inside a clear plastic bag held loosely at the wrist by a hair band, and a steel tumbler inside another bag beside it.
setup.caption: 2. One bag on your hand, one on the tumbler. Keep the bands loose.

setup.art: A close-up of the inside of the hand bag, misty with tiny drops, next to the clear, dry tumbler bag.
setup.caption: 3. Look every 5 minutes. Which bag changes?

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: A little misty near the fingers
Drops on the plastic, hand feels damp

flow.do: 1. Your child washes and dries their hands well with a towel. 2. Wait two minutes. 3. Ask them to touch their palm to their cheek.
flow.say: First, let's make sure your hand is really dry. Dry it well and wait. Now touch your cheek with your palm. Does it feel wet or dry?
flow.kid: Dry your hands well. Wait two minutes. Touch your cheek. Wet or dry?
flow.parent: The hand should feel dry. That is the point: we start with a hand that seems to give out nothing.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Hidden Water Test. You check that your hand feels completely dry.

flow.do: 1. Show the two bags and the tumbler. 2. Explain the plan. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason for each bag. 4. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: One bag will go over your hand. The other goes over this empty tumbler. In 15 minutes, what will each bag look like inside? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One bag on your hand. One on the tumbler. What will each look like? Why?

good: My hand is dry, so nothing will happen.
My hand is warm, so maybe it will make the bag steamy.
The tumbler is not alive, so nothing will come out of it.

flow.parent: Do not hint. Many children guess nothing will happen, because the hand feels dry. Any guess with a reason is good.

flow.do: 1. Slide one bag over your child's hand. 2. Close it at the wrist with a loose band, one finger can slip under it. 3. Put the tumbler in the other bag, closed the same way.
flow.say: Let's put the bags on. The band must be loose. Can you slip a finger under it? Good.
flow.kid: Put your hand in the bag. Keep the band loose. Put the tumbler in the other bag.
flow.parent: Never tight. The bag only needs to stop air rushing in. Keep the child away from the fan and from sunlight, because both would change the result.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits still with the hand resting on the table. 2. Look at both bags at 5, 10 and 15 minutes. 3. Write what you see each time.
flow.say: Sit still and rest your hand. We will look every 5 minutes. Tell me exactly what you see on the plastic.
flow.kid: Sit still. Look at both bags every 5 minutes. What do you see?
flow.parent: By 5 minutes the hand bag usually looks a little misty near the fingers. By 10 to 15 minutes there are tiny drops, and the hand feels damp. The tumbler bag stays clear. In an AC room or on a cold day it can take 20 minutes. While you wait, read the five needs cards together.

flow.do: 1. Take off both bags. 2. Your child feels the inside of each one with a dry finger. 3. Compare them.
flow.say: Take the bags off. Feel inside each one with a dry finger. Which one is wet? Where did that water come from?
flow.kid: Take off the bags. Feel inside each. Which one is wet? Why?

check.q: The hand bag turned misty, but the tumbler bag stayed clear. Where did the water come from?
options: From the air in the room
From the skin of the hand
check.why: Both bags had the same room air and the same kind of plastic, but only the hand bag misted. So the water came from the skin. Picking 'the air in the room' is a sensible first guess. But then the tumbler bag would have misted too, and it did not.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw, and why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why does it matter for your body?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer: My skin gives out water even when it feels dry. The hand bag misted and dripped, but the tumbler bag stayed clear. My body is losing water all the time, so I need to drink every day. Scientists call this insensible perspiration, which means sweat you cannot sense.
flow.think: If you did 20 jumps first, would the bag mist faster or slower? Try it another day.

experiments.title: The Water Ring: can a moat keep ants off the sugar?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put out two small caps of sugar where ants walk. One sits on a dry plate. The other sits on a little island in a ring of water. You see which one the ants reach.
experiments.question: Ants need food, and they come to our kitchens for it. Can a ring of water around the sugar stop them reaching it?
experiments.predict: Which sugar cap will the ants reach: the one on the dry plate, the one inside the water ring, or both? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both caps hold the same amount of the same sugar. Both stand in the same place, about 30 cm apart, near where ants walk. Both are checked at the same times. Only one thing is different: one cap has a ring of water around it. Nothing may touch the island from outside, or the ants could use it as a bridge.
results_table: Ants in the water or at its edge

materials.item: two plastic bottle caps, each with half a teaspoon of sugar. A pinch of jaggery or a drop of honey works too.
two steel plates
one small steel katori or cup, turned upside down, to be the island
a tumbler of water
a clock, a notebook and a pencil, and a magnifying glass if you have one
a damp cloth, for cleaning up at the end

experiments.safety: Do not kill or hurt the ants. Some ants bite, so watch without touching them. Wash your hands after cleaning up.

schedule.what: Set up two sugar caps near an ant path, one on a dry plate and one in a water ring. Check at 30 minutes and at 1 to 2 hours. Clean up and explain.

experiments.record: Count the ants on each cap at each check and write the numbers in the table. Draw both plates at the last check.

setup.art: A line of small ants walking along the edge of a kitchen counter, with a child pointing at them.
setup.caption: 1. Find a place where ants walk.

setup.art: Two steel plates on a kitchen floor: one with a bottle cap of sugar on it, the other with an upturned katori in a ring of water and a bottle cap of sugar on top of the katori.
setup.caption: 2. One cap on a dry plate. One on an island in water.

setup.art: Ants crowding round the sugar on the dry plate, and the sugar on the water island with no ants, a few ants stopped at the edge of the water.
setup.caption: 3. Count the ants on each cap.

flow.do: 1. Look for ants together: along the kitchen counter, near the sink, by the dustbin or along a window frame. 2. Watch one ant for a minute.
flow.say: Ants are always looking for food for their colony, the big family in their nest. Let's find where they walk. Watch one ant. Where is she going?
flow.kid: Find ants. Watch one ant for a minute. Where is she going?
flow.parent: Worker ants are all females, so 'she' is right. Their colony has to feed the queen and the young ants in the nest, so workers search for food all day. If you cannot find ants, put the plates near the kitchen counter or a window and leave them overnight.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Water Ring test. You find where the ants in your home walk.

flow.do: 1. Put half a teaspoon of sugar in each cap. 2. Put one cap on a dry plate. 3. Turn the katori upside down in the middle of the other plate. 4. Pour water round it, about 1 cm deep. 5. Put the second cap on top of the katori.
flow.say: This sugar sits on a dry plate. This one sits on an island with a moat of water round it, like a fort. Make sure nothing touches the island.
flow.kid: Put sugar in both caps. One on a dry plate. One on the island in water.
flow.parent: Check that the island is dry on top and that no spoon, cloth or wall touches it. Put the two plates about 30 cm apart, both near the ant path.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason, and write it down.
flow.say: Which sugar will the ants reach first? Will they reach the island at all? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which sugar will the ants find? Why do you think so?

good: Ants can't swim, so the water will stop them.
Ants are clever and will find a way across.
The ants will smell both, so they will try both.

flow.parent: Do not say what will happen. A child who thinks the ants will get across is making a fair guess. Some ants can cross water if there is a bridge.

flow.do: After 30 minutes, count the ants on each cap and at the edge of the water. Use the magnifying glass if you have one.
flow.say: Let's count. How many ants are on each cap? Is any ant at the edge of the water? What is she doing?
flow.kid: Count the ants on each cap. Are any at the water? What are they doing?
flow.parent: There may be only a few ants at first. Scouts find food, then lay a scent trail that brings many more. By 1 to 2 hours the dry plate usually has many ants and the island has none. Ants at the water's edge often turn back.

flow.do: Check again after 1 to 2 hours. Count and write the numbers. If ants reached the island, look for a bridge: a crumb, a thread or a wet patch.
flow.say: Count again. Did the numbers change? Did any ant reach the island? If one did, how did she get there?
flow.kid: Count again. Did any ant reach the island? How?

check.q: Ants crowded the sugar on the dry plate but did not reach the sugar on the island. Why?
options: The island sugar did not smell sweet
The ring of water stopped them walking to it
The ants did not like that cap
check.why: Both caps held the same sugar, so the only difference was the water. Most house ants will not cross water, and a small ant can get stuck on the water's surface. Picking 'did not smell sweet' is a fair idea, but it was the same sugar in the same kind of cap.

flow.do: 1. Your child says what they think, what they saw, and why. 2. Put the sugar away. 3. Wipe the ant trail with a damp cloth. 4. Wash hands.
flow.say: Tell me what you think, what you saw, and why. Then let's put the sugar away and wipe their trail, so the ants go back to look outside.
flow.kid: Say what you think, what you saw and why. Then clean up.
flow.parent: A good answer: A ring of water keeps ants away from food. The dry-plate sugar had many ants and the island had none. Ants needed the food, but they could not walk across water. This is why many Indian families stand a sugar dabba or a food cupboard's legs in a dish of water. Wiping the trail removes the scent that guides the ants.
flow.think: The ants came because they needed food, just as you do. Where else could they find food, outside your home?

activities.title: Hold and Wait: can you save up a breath?
activities.context: This is a starting activity. You hold your breath for a short time, sitting down, and notice that your body soon makes you breathe again.

materials.item: a chair or a mat to sit on
a clock or phone timer

activities.safety: Always sit down. Never hold your breath in water, and never make anyone else hold theirs. Stop as soon as you want to breathe.

schedule.what: Hold your breath after a normal breath, sitting down, and count. Talk about why we cannot save up air.

activities.record: Write how many seconds you held your breath. Write one sentence: why do I have to keep breathing?

setup.art: A girl sitting on a mat, holding her breath with puffed cheeks, while her mother watches a phone timer.
setup.caption: 1. Sit down. Take a normal breath and hold it.

setup.art: The same girl breathing out with relief, holding up fingers to show a number.
setup.caption: 2. Breathe when you want to. How many seconds was it?

flow.do: 1. Your child sits down. 2. They take a normal breath and hold it. 3. Count the seconds aloud. 4. They stop as soon as they want to.
flow.say: Sit down. Take a normal breath and hold it. I will count. Breathe again as soon as you want to.
flow.kid: Sit down. Take a normal breath. Hold it. Breathe when you want to.
flow.parent: Most children hold for 15 to 40 seconds. Do not make it a contest. The point is that the body makes you breathe again very soon.
flow.context: This is a short starting activity for the basic needs unit. You notice how quickly your body needs air again.

flow.do: Talk about it: you could save a snack, and you can wait for a drink. Why can't you save up air?
flow.say: You can save a laddu for later. You can wait an hour for a drink. But you can't wait a minute for air. Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: You can save a snack. Why can't you save up air?

ask.q: Why can't we save up air?
good: My body uses air all the time.
There is no space inside to keep it.
Every part of me needs air every minute.

flow.parent: Do not explain yet. The explanation card on air comes later. Accept every idea, and ask your child to remember theirs.

activities.title: Need or Want? The sorting slips
activities.context: In this activity you sort slips of paper into needs and wants, then argue about the hard ones.

materials.item: 16 small slips of paper and a pencil
two bowls, labelled NEED and WANT

schedule.what: Sort 16 things into needs and wants, and argue about the hard ones.

activities.record: Write the three hardest slips and the reason you chose for each one.

setup.art: Sixteen paper slips spread on a floor, with words like 'drinking water', 'chocolate', 'roof', 'mobile phone' and 'sweater'.
setup.caption: 1. Write one thing on each slip.

setup.art: Two steel bowls labelled NEED and WANT with paper slips in each, and three slips left in the middle marked with a question mark.
setup.caption: 2. Sort them. Put the hard ones in the middle.

flow.do: Write one thing on each slip. Use these 16: drinking water, rice, a roof, a toy car, a cotton shirt, a sweater, chocolate, a fan. Then: soap, a mobile phone, a blanket, a TV, fresh air, a bicycle, medicine, a friend.
flow.say: Here are 16 things. Some we cannot live without. Some are nice to have. Let's write one on each slip.
flow.kid: Write one thing on each slip.
flow.context: This is a sorting activity. You decide which things are needs and which are wants.

flow.do: Your child puts each slip in the NEED bowl or the WANT bowl and gives a reason. Hard ones go in the middle.
flow.say: Put each one in a bowl. Tell me why. If you can't decide, put it in the middle.
flow.kid: Put each slip in NEED or WANT. Say why. Hard ones go in the middle.
flow.parent: Expect arguments about the fan, the sweater, medicine and the friend. That is good. A strong answer gives a reason: 'A sweater is a need in Ooty in December, but a want in Chennai in May.'

flow.do: Talk about the slips in the middle.
flow.say: Let's look at the middle ones. When would each one be a need? When would it be a want?
flow.kid: Look at the middle slips. When is each one a need?

check.q: Medicine is in the middle. When is it a need?
options: When a person is ill and the medicine keeps them well
Never, it is always a want
check.why: A healthy person does not need medicine. A person with an illness, such as diabetes, may need medicine every day to stay alive. So whether a thing is a need can depend on the person.

activities.title: The Mosquito Hunt: find still water at home
activities.context: In this activity you search your home and balcony for still water, where mosquitoes could lay their eggs, and empty it.

materials.item: a torch
a notebook and pencil
an old cloth

activities.safety: Do not lean over a balcony railing. A grown-up empties or moves heavy things such as a cooler or a big bucket.

schedule.what: Search for still water in the home and on the balcony. Empty it, and make a weekly checklist.

activities.record: Make a list of every place you found still water. Tick each one when it has been emptied.

setup.art: A child shining a torch into a clay flower-pot plate on a balcony, with still water in it.
setup.caption: 1. Look in plates, trays, buckets and coolers.

setup.art: A child tipping water out of a flower-pot plate into a drain, with a grown-up nearby.
setup.caption: 2. Empty it, and turn the plate upside down if it is not needed.

flow.do: Search together: flower-pot plates, the tray under the fridge, buckets, a cooler, old bottles and tins on the balcony, a blocked drain.
flow.say: Mosquitoes lay their eggs in still water. The young ones grow there in about a week. Let's hunt for any still water in our home.
flow.kid: Hunt for still water. Look in plates, trays and buckets.
flow.parent: Young mosquitoes, called larvae or wrigglers, look like tiny threads that wriggle up and down. If you find them, show your child, then empty the water into a drain. Dengue mosquitoes breed in small amounts of clean, still water, even a bottle cap's worth.
flow.context: This is a home hunt. You look for still water where mosquitoes could breed.

flow.do: 1. Empty every place you found. 2. Make a weekly checklist and stick it on the fridge.
flow.say: Let's empty them all. Then we'll make a list, so we check every week. Why every week?
flow.kid: Empty them. Make a list. Why check every week?

ask.q: Why do we need to check every week?
good: Young mosquitoes grow up in about a week, so emptying every week stops them before they fly.
Water collects again when it rains or when we water the plants.

activities.title: The Breeze Path: does air need a way in and a way out?
activities.context: In this activity you hold a paper strip at a window to see whether air flows through a room with one opening, and then with two.

materials.item: a strip of tissue paper or thin newspaper, about 20 cm long, taped to a pencil
a room with two windows, or a window and a door, on different sides

activities.safety: Stay away from the window edge on high floors. A grown-up opens and closes windows.

schedule.what: Hold a paper strip at a window, first with one opening, then with two. Compare.

activities.record: Draw the room from above. Draw arrows to show where the air went with one opening, and with two.

setup.art: A child holding a paper strip on a pencil near an open window, with the room's door closed, the strip hanging down.
setup.caption: 1. One opening only. Watch the strip.

setup.art: The same child with the door on the other side open, and the strip blowing out sideways.
setup.caption: 2. Open a second opening across the room. Watch again.

flow.do: 1. Close all windows and doors of one room, and switch off the fan. 2. Open one window. 3. Your child holds the paper strip in the window gap for one minute.
flow.say: Fresh air must come into a room, and used air must go out. Let's see if air flows with only one window open. Watch the strip.
flow.kid: Hold the strip at the open window. Does it move?
flow.context: This is an activity about ventilation. You find out whether air flows better through a room with one opening or two.

flow.do: 1. Now open a door or window on the other side of the room. 2. Hold the strip in the first window again for one minute.
flow.say: Now there's a way in and a way out. Hold the strip in the same place. What does it do now?
flow.kid: Now open another window. Hold the strip again. What happens?
flow.parent: With one opening, the strip usually hangs or only flutters. With an opening across the room, it often blows steadily, in or out. This is called cross-ventilation. On a still day the difference is small, so try again in the evening, when a breeze often picks up.

flow.do: Talk about the kitchen: where can smoke and steam get out?
flow.say: Where does the smoke from cooking go in our kitchen? Is there a way in and a way out for the air?
flow.kid: Look at the kitchen. How does smoke get out?

check.q: Why does a room with windows on two sides get fresher air?
options: Air can come in one side and go out the other
Two windows let in more sunlight, and sunlight makes air
check.why: Air needs a way in and a way out to keep flowing. With one opening, the room's air mostly stays where it is. Sunlight is good for a home, but it does not make air.

activities.title: Dress for the Day: clothes for three places
activities.context: In this activity you draw clothes for a child in three places and weathers, and give a reason for each choice.

materials.item: a sheet of paper folded into three parts, pencils and crayons
a few real clothes to feel: a cotton shirt, a woollen sweater, a raincoat or umbrella

schedule.what: Feel three kinds of clothes. Draw a child dressed for Chennai in May, Ooty in December and Kochi in the monsoon.

activities.record: Under each drawing, write one reason for the clothes you chose.

setup.art: A cotton shirt, a woollen sweater and a raincoat laid on a bed side by side.
setup.caption: 1. Feel each one. What is it made of?

setup.art: A sheet folded in three with a child drawn in a cotton shirt in sun, in a sweater and cap in mist, and in a raincoat in rain.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a child dressed for each place.

flow.do: Your child feels each piece of clothing, holds it up to the light, and breathes through it gently.
flow.say: Feel each one. Hold it up to the light. Which one lets air through? Which one feels thick and fluffy? Which one is smooth and shiny?
flow.kid: Feel each one. Which lets air through? Which is thick?
flow.context: This is a drawing activity about clothes for different weather.

flow.do: Your child draws a child in Chennai in May, Ooty in December and Kochi in the monsoon. They write a reason under each.
flow.say: Draw a child in each place. What would keep them comfortable and safe? Write why.
flow.kid: Draw a child in each place. Write why you chose those clothes.
flow.parent: Good reasons: cotton soaks up sweat and lets air pass, so the body cools. Wool traps still air, which slows heat leaving the body. A raincoat stops rain soaking the clothes, because wet clothes make you cold.

activities.title: Who Else Lives Here? The other beings in our home
activities.context: In this activity you look for the other living beings who share your home, and work out which of their needs your home meets.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a torch

activities.safety: Look, but do not touch insects, spiders or lizards. Do not move a bird's nest.

schedule.what: Find other living beings in the home and on the balcony, and say which of their needs the home meets.

activities.record: Make a table: who I found, where, and which needs our home meets for them.

setup.art: A child with a torch looking at a gecko behind a picture frame on a wall.
setup.caption: 1. Look for other living beings at home.

setup.art: A child's notebook with a table: ants, gecko, tulsi plant, pigeon, with ticks under food, water and shelter.
setup.caption: 2. Write which needs our home meets for them.

flow.do: Look together in every room. Check for ants in the kitchen and a gecko on the wall at night. Look for a spider in a corner, potted plants, and a pigeon or crow at the window.
flow.say: We share our home with others. Let's find them. Who lives here besides us?
flow.kid: Find others who live in our home. Look high and low.
flow.context: This activity is about the other living beings who share our home and their needs.

flow.do: For each one, ask which needs the home meets: food, water, shelter or warmth.
flow.say: Why does the gecko live here? What does she find on our wall? What do the ants find in our kitchen?
flow.kid: Why does each one live here? What do they find?
flow.parent: Good answers: the gecko finds insects near the lights and a safe place behind the frame. The ants find crumbs and sugar. The tulsi plant gets water from us and light from the window. Our home meets their needs as well as ours.

projects.title: Our Home Care Week: one need each day
projects.context: This is a 5-day project. Each day you check how well your home takes care of one basic need, and fix one thing.

materials.item: a chart paper or a large sheet, and sketch pens
a torch
a plate, a katori and water, from the Water Ring test

projects.safety: A grown-up handles the gas stove, the exhaust fan, heavy buckets and anything on a balcony ledge.

schedule.what: Air day: check that each room has a window that opens and that the kitchen has a window or exhaust fan. Open the windows for 10 minutes.
Water day: check that drinking water is covered and taken out with a ladle or tap. Empty any still water.
Food day: check that food is covered. Stand the sugar dabba in a plate of water if ants come.
Clothes day: wash a handkerchief and dry it in the sun. Check that damp towels are hung out to dry.
Home day: check the drains and the bin. Then make a poster of the five needs and how our family cares for each.

projects.record: Each day, write one thing that was already good and one thing you fixed. On day 5, make the poster.

setup.art: A chart paper on a wall divided into five boxes labelled Air, Water, Food, Clothes and Home, with ticks in two of them.
setup.caption: 1. Make a chart with five boxes, one for each day.

setup.art: A child standing a steel sugar dabba in a plate of water on a kitchen shelf.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, check one need and fix one thing.

flow.do: Air day. Walk through each room with your child. Does each room have a window that opens? Is there a way for kitchen smoke to leave?
flow.say: Today is air day. Let's check every room. Can fresh air come in? Can used air go out?
flow.kid: Air day. Check each room. Can fresh air get in?
flow.context: This is the first day of Our Home Care Week. Each day you check one basic need at home.

flow.do: Water day. Check the drinking water: is it covered? Do people dip tumblers in with their hands? Empty any still water.
flow.say: Today is water day. Is our drinking water covered? How do we take it out? Is there any still water for mosquitoes?
flow.kid: Water day. Is the drinking water covered? Any still water?
flow.parent: A ladle with a long handle, or a pot with a tap, keeps hands out of the water.

flow.do: Food day. Check that cooked food and dabbas are covered. If ants come, stand the sugar dabba in a plate of water.
flow.say: Today is food day. Is our food covered from flies, ants and dust? What did the Water Ring test teach us?
flow.kid: Food day. Is our food covered? Can ants get in?

flow.do: Clothes day. Your child washes a handkerchief with soap, rinses it and hangs it in the sun.
flow.say: Today is clothes day. Let's wash this hanky and dry it in the sun. Why do you think we dry clothes in the sun?
flow.kid: Clothes day. Wash a hanky. Dry it in the sun.
flow.parent: Sunlight dries clothes fast, and strong sunlight also kills many germs. Damp clothes left folded can smell and grow mould.

flow.do: Home day. Check the drains and the bin together. Then make a poster with the five needs and how your family cares for each one.
flow.say: Today is home day. Is the bin covered? Does water drain away? Now let's make our poster.
flow.kid: Home day. Check the bin and the drain. Make the poster.

challenges.title: The Clean Water Corner
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You plan a corner of the kitchen where a family's drinking water stays clean all day.
challenges.problem: Design a way to keep a day's drinking water for your family clean. Dust, flies, mosquitoes and dirty hands must not get into it, and everyone must be able to take a drink easily.
constraints: Use only things most homes have, or can buy cheaply.
A child must be able to get a drink without help.
No hand or tumbler may go into the water.
materials: a steel pot with a lid, or a clean bucket with a lid
paper and pencil for the design
general: A covered steel pot with a long-handled ladle hanging beside it.
A clay matka or steel container with a small tap near the bottom.
Clean steel bottles filled each morning, one for each person.
creative: Tie a clean cotton cloth over the mouth of the pot, so even fine dust stays out.
Put a picture label on the ladle hook, so small children know to use it.
Keep the corner on a high shelf away from the stove and the bin.
challenges.your_turn: Now draw your own clean water corner for your home. Label how it keeps out dust, insects and hands. Then set it up with a grown-up and use it for a day.

setup.art: A child drawing a plan of a kitchen corner with a covered pot, a ladle on a hook and tumblers on a shelf.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your design.

setup.art: A real kitchen corner with a covered steel pot, a long ladle hanging from a hook and clean tumblers upside down.
setup.caption: 2. Set it up and use it for a day.

constraints: One bag only, that a grown-up can carry.
It must cover water, food, clothes and shelter for every person in the family.
It must include anything a family member needs every day, such as medicine.
materials: a school bag, to see how much fits

A copy of important papers in a waterproof bag.
creative: Pack each person's clothes in a separate plastic bag, so they stay dry.
Add a small toy or book for a little child, because comfort helps people stay calm.
Make a list on the bag of what to add at the last minute, such as phones and fresh water.
challenges.your_turn: Now make the list for your own family. Show it to a grown-up and ask what they would add.
