quiz.p: Which three basic needs keep us alive?
opts: Air, water and food
Clothes, a home and toys
Food, a TV and a fan
quiz.why: Without air, water or food a person dies. Clothes and a home keep us safe and healthy, so they are needs too, but people can survive a short time without them.

quiz.p: Which one is a want, not a need?
opts: Drinking water
A roof over your head
A new video game
Food
quiz.why: A video game is fun but not needed to live or stay well. Water, a roof and food are needs.

quiz.p: In the Hidden Water Test, the bag on the dry hand misted up. What did that show?
opts: The plastic makes water
The skin gives out water even when it feels dry
Room air always makes bags misty
quiz.why: The tumbler bag in the same room stayed clear, so the water came from the skin. Picking 'room air' is a sensible guess, but then both bags would have misted.

quiz.p: When you breathe out, which gas do you give out more of than you took in?
opts: Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
Air has no gases
quiz.why: Your cells make carbon dioxide as they use food for energy. Breathed-out air has much more carbon dioxide than room air, and less oxygen.

opts: Only to look nice
To protect our skin from sun, cold, insects and dirt
Because clothes make heat
quiz.why: Clothes protect the skin and help the body stay at the right temperature. Looking nice is a want. Wool keeps you warm by trapping still air, not by making heat.

quiz.p: Which is the best way to keep drinking water safe at home?
opts: Leave it open so it gets fresh air
Keep it covered and pour it with a ladle
Dip a tumbler in with your hand
quiz.why: A lid keeps out dust and insects. A ladle keeps fingers out of the water everyone drinks.

quiz.p: Why should flower-pot plates be emptied once a week?
opts: So mosquitoes cannot breed in the still water
So the plant does not get bored
Because water goes bad in one day
quiz.why: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water, and the young grow there in about a week. Emptying the water every week stops them before they can fly.

quiz.p: In the Water Ring test, the ants reached the sugar on the dry plate but not on the island. Why?
opts: The island sugar was a different kind
Most ants will not cross water
Ants do not like bottle caps
quiz.why: Both caps had the same sugar. Only the water was different, and most house ants turn back at water.

quiz.p: A woollen sweater is a need in Shimla in winter. In Chennai in May it is:
opts: Still a need
A want
Dangerous
quiz.why: Whether a thing is a need can depend on the place and the weather. In Chennai's heat, a sweater is not needed.

quiz.p: What makes a room have good ventilation?
opts: Keeping every window shut
Openings on different sides, so air can come in and go out
A bright light
quiz.why: Air keeps flowing only when it has a way in and a way out. Windows on two sides, or an exhaust fan, let used air leave.

quiz.p: What did Santorio find with his weighing chair?
opts: That the body loses a lot of water we cannot see
That food makes us heavier forever
That breathing does nothing
quiz.why: Santorio found that much of what he ate and drank left his body unseen, through his skin and breath. He called it insensible perspiration.

quiz.p: Why can a person live weeks without food but only minutes without air?
opts: Food is less important than air
The body stores food as fat, but stores almost no oxygen
Air is heavier than food
quiz.why: The body can use stored fat for energy for weeks. But it holds very little oxygen, and every cell needs oxygen all the time.

items.p: Match each basic need to one thing it does for us.
pairs: carries food and oxygen in our blood
gives energy to move and grow
protect our skin from sun, cold and insects
keeps off rain, wind and animals
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each need has its own main job. A strong answer can say the job in their own words, not only match it.

items.p: Without which of these can a person live for the shortest time?
opts: Food
Water
Air
A home
items.why: A person can live only a few minutes without air, a few days without water and a few weeks without food. The body stores some food and water, but almost no oxygen. That is why you could not save up a breath.

items.p: Sort these into needs and wants for a child living in Chennai.
items.a: see items
items.why: Water, food, clothes and a roof keep the child alive and well. The game, chocolate and bat are nice but not needed. A sweater is a want in Chennai's warm weather, though it would be a need in Shimla in winter.

items.p: Remember the Hidden Water Test, where one plastic bag went over a dry hand and another over an empty tumbler. Why did we use a tumbler bag at all?
items.a: The tumbler bag had the same air and the same plastic, but no hand. It stayed clear. That showed the mist did not come from the room's air or the plastic, so it must have come from the hand.
items.why: A strong answer says the tumbler bag is the comparison: everything the same except the hand.

items.p: If your skin feels dry, your body is not losing any water.
items.why: False. In the Hidden Water Test, a dry hand misted up a plastic bag within minutes. Skin and breath let water out all the time, even when you cannot feel it.

items.p: We breathe in air for the gas called ____, and we breathe out ____.
items.why: Our cells need oxygen to get energy from food. They make carbon dioxide, which the blood carries back to the lungs to be breathed out.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 3, finds a flower-pot plate full of still water on her balcony. Why should she empty it?
opts: The water will make the plant grow too fast
Mosquitoes can lay eggs in it
The water will turn into air
items.why: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water, and the young grow there in about a week. Some mosquitoes spread dengue and malaria. Emptying still water every week stops them.

items.p: Arjun says, "I don't need to drink water today, because I'm not sweating." What would you tell him? Use your own test.
items.a: I would tell him his body loses water even without sweating. In my test, a bag on my dry hand turned misty and dripped. Water also leaves in every breath and in urine. So he needs to drink every day.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence from the bag test, not only a rule.

items.p: Three of these keep drinking water clean. One makes it dirty. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Keeping the pot covered
Taking water out with a ladle
Dipping a tumbler in with your hand
Boiling the water and letting it cool covered
items.why: Covering, using a ladle and boiling all keep germs out of water. Dipping a tumbler in with your hand puts germs from your fingers into the water everyone drinks.

items.p: Draw a room in a flat from above, with two windows on opposite sides. Draw arrows to show how fresh air comes in and used air goes out.
items.a: A square room with a window on each side. Arrows come in through one window, cross the room and go out through the other.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a way in and a way out. Air keeps flowing only when it has both.
items.art: A blank square for the room, seen from above, with space around it.

items.p: Why do farmers in hot places often wear loose cotton clothes?
opts: Cotton is heavy, so the wind can't blow it away
Cotton soaks up sweat and lets air pass, so the body can cool
Cotton makes heat for the body
items.why: In hot weather the body cools as sweat dries. Loose cotton soaks up sweat and lets air move past the skin, so the sweat dries and cools the body.

items.p: Put these in order, starting with the air going into your nose.
items: Your cells use the oxygen to get energy from food
You breathe in through your nose
a: You breathe in through your nose
Your cells use the oxygen to get energy from food
items.why: Air goes in through the nose to the lungs. Oxygen passes into the blood, and the blood carries it to every cell.

items.p: Ants in a kitchen are a sign that the home must be dirty.
items.why: False. Ants search for food all day, because their colony needs it. One grain of sugar in a very clean kitchen is enough to bring them.

items.p: Label this kitchen to show how each need is cared for: covered water pot, ladle, food dabba in a plate of water, open window, covered bin.
items.a: The covered water pot with the ladle beside it. The dabba standing in a plate of water. The window open for air. The bin with a lid.
items.why: Each label shows one way of keeping a need clean: water, food, air and home.
items.art: An unlabelled drawing of a small Indian kitchen with five blank label lines.

items.p: Name one thing that is a need in Ooty in December but a want in Chennai in May. Explain why.
items.a: A woollen sweater. In Ooty in December it is cold, and the sweater traps still air and slows heat leaving the body. In Chennai in May it is hot, so a sweater is not needed.
items.why: A strong answer names the thing and gives the reason from the weather.

items.p: Three people talk about whether a ceiling fan is a need or a want.

views.says: It's a need. In May the flat is so hot that I can't sleep without it.

views.who: Revathi, Divya's grandmother, who grew up in a village
views.says: It's a want. We slept on the terrace in summer, with no fan, and we were fine.
For most people it's a want. But in a heatwave, a fan can protect the health of a baby or an old person.

items.ask: Who do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then say one thing the person you disagree with gets right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, for example: I agree with the doctor, because the answer depends on who it is and how hot it is. Then it gives the other side its due, for example: Revathi is right that people lived without fans, but a terrace is cooler than a closed flat.
items.why: This is a real question with no single answer. Whether something is a need can depend on the person, the place and the weather.

items.p: Kavya puts a bag over her hand. After 10 minutes she sees drops inside. Then she does 20 jumps and tries again. What will most likely happen?
opts: No mist at all, because she is tired
The mist comes faster, because a warm, working body loses more water
The mist comes exactly as fast as before
items.why: When you exercise, your body warms up and sweats to cool down, so more water leaves the skin. The bag mists faster. This is why you need to drink more after playing.

items.p: In the Water Ring test, Meera's ants reached the sugar on the island. She finds a long thread lying from the floor up onto the katori. What happened, and how should she fix her test?
items.a: The thread made a bridge over the water, so the ants walked across it. She should remove the thread, check that nothing touches the island, and try again.
items.why: A strong answer spots the bridge and says how to make the test fair again: only the water should differ.

items.p: A child at rest breathes about 20 times a minute. About how many times does a child breathe in one hour?
items.why: There are 60 minutes in an hour. 20 breaths times 60 minutes is 1,200 breaths. You do this every hour, awake or asleep, without thinking.

items.p: Ayesha's family keeps the sugar tin standing in a plate of water. Why does this work?
opts: The water makes the sugar taste bad to ants
Most ants will not cross water, so they cannot reach the tin
The water cools the sugar so ants can't smell it
items.why: Most house ants turn back at water, and a small ant can be trapped on the water's surface. As long as nothing makes a bridge, the ants cannot reach the tin.

items.p: Your body stores some food as fat and some water, but almost no air. Use this to explain why a person can live for weeks without food but only minutes without air.
items.a: When there is no food, the body can use its stored fat for energy for weeks. But it keeps very little oxygen, and every cell needs oxygen all the time. So without air the oxygen runs out in a few minutes.
items.why: A strong answer links each time to how much of that need the body can store.

items.p: Sort these by which basic need they help take care of.
items: an exhaust fan in the kitchen
a lid on the water pot
a mesh cover over the dal
items.a: see items
items.why: Fans and windows give fresh air. Lids and emptying still water keep water clean and stop mosquitoes. Covers and washing keep food safe.

items.p: Draw how water leaves your body during one day. Show at least three ways.
items.a: A child with arrows showing water leaving as breath from the mouth and nose, as sweat or unseen water from the skin, and as urine. A strong drawing may also show tears.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that water leaves in more than one way, including ways we do not notice, such as breath and dry skin.
items.art: A blank outline of a child's body.

items.p: A cool room with the AC on and the windows shut always has fresh air.
items.why: False. Most home ACs cool the same room air again and again. With the windows shut, the carbon dioxide from everyone's breath builds up. Opening a window for a while lets fresh air in.

items.p: Water that stays still for days, where mosquitoes can lay eggs, is called ____ water.
items.why: Stagnant means still and not flowing. Mosquito eggs hatch in it, and the young grow there in about a week.

items.p: Paati, an old woman, has a headache on a hot afternoon. Her water bottle is still full. What is the most likely reason?
opts: She drank too much water
She has not drunk enough, and her body is short of water
The bottle is too heavy
items.why: A headache can be a sign of dehydration. Older people often feel less thirsty, so they may forget to drink even when their body needs water.

items.p: Why must clothes be washed and dried, not just worn again and again?
items.a: Sweat and dirt build up in clothes. Germs and mould can grow in damp, dirty cloth and harm the skin. Washing removes them, and drying in the sun stops mould and kills many germs.
items.why: A strong answer says what builds up in clothes and what washing and drying do about it.

items.p: Match each home to the place it suits.
pairs: a place with heavy rain or snow
a city flat that needs a breeze
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each home is built to protect people from the main danger of its place: floods, rain and snow, heat, or still air.

items.p: Three of these are basic needs for every person. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: Air
Water
A mobile phone
Food
items.why: Air, water and food keep every person alive. A phone can be very useful, but people live well without one, so it is a want for most people.

items.p: A crow sits on a balcony railing in May with her beak open, panting. Which of her needs is she having trouble meeting? What could you do?
items.a: She is hot and probably needs water. Birds pant to lose heat, and that also loses water. I could put out a shallow bowl of clean water and change it every day.
items.why: A strong answer names the need and a kind, safe way to help. Changing the water daily stops mosquitoes breeding in it.

worksheets.title: Needs, Wants and the Body That Leaks (challenge)

items.p: In 1943, a psychologist and later researchers disagreed about the order of our needs.

views.who: Abraham Maslow, a psychologist in the USA
views.says: People meet their needs in order: first food and water, then safety, then love and friends, then respect.

views.who: Researchers who studied people in 123 countries in 2011
views.says: Needs work side by side. Many people who are poor and often hungry still feel loved and respected, and that matters to their happiness at the same time.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? Give an example from life. Then say what the other view gets right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with an example, such as a poor family who are hungry but laugh together and love each other. Then it gives the other view its due: a person who is starving does think mostly about food.
items.why: Both views see something true. The body's needs are urgent, but people need love and respect even while those needs are not fully met.

items.p: Santorio, a doctor in Italy 400 years ago, weighed his food and drink, and everything that came out of him as urine and stools. The waste weighed much less than what went in, yet his own weight stayed about the same. Where did the rest go? How does your bag test help you answer?
items.a: The rest left his body unseen, as water through his skin and in his breath. My bag test showed it: a dry hand misted up a bag within minutes. So water leaves the skin all the time, even when you cannot feel it.
items.why: A strong answer joins Santorio's numbers to the child's own evidence, the misty bag.

items.p: Farhan wants to test whether ants will cross a ring of salty water as well as plain water. Which test is fair?
opts: One plate with salty water and one with plain water, the same sugar on both islands, side by side
Salty water today, plain water next week in a different room
Salty water with sugar, plain water with jaggery
items.why: In a fair test only one thing changes: here, the kind of water. The sugar, the place and the time stay the same. Changing the day, the room or the food as well would make the result impossible to explain.

items.p: A family in a flood has plenty of water all around them, but they still need drinking water to be brought in. Explain why.
items.a: Flood water is mixed with mud, sewage and germs, so it is not safe to drink. It can spread cholera and diarrhoea. The family needs clean drinking water, boiled or bottled, even though water is all around.
items.why: A strong answer says the difference between water and safe drinking water, and why flood water is unsafe.

items.p: Santorio wrote that if a person takes in 8 pounds of food and drink in a day, about 5 pounds leave unseen. How many pounds leave in ways you can see?
items.why: 8 minus 5 is 3. So about 3 pounds leave as urine and stools, and more than half leaves unseen through the skin and breath. A pound is an old unit of weight, a little less than half a kilogram.

items.p: Design an ant-proof stand for a jar of jaggery. Draw it and label the part that stops the ants.
items.a: A drawing of a jar on a small stand, with the stand's legs in bowls of water, or the jar on an island in a plate of water. The water is labelled as the part that stops the ants. A strong design makes sure nothing touches the jar from outside.
items.why: A strong design uses the water barrier from the Water Ring test and avoids any bridge.
items.art: A blank box with a jar drawn in the middle.

items.p: Ants came to the sugar because their colony needed food. Is it fair to keep the sugar from them? Give your view and a reason, and say what the ants could eat instead.
items.a: A strong answer gives a view with a reason. For example: yes, because people need the sugar and ants in food can bring dirt. The ants can find food outside, such as dead insects, seeds and the sweet juice of plants. The water ring keeps them out without hurting them.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A strong answer thinks about both the family's needs and the ants' needs.

items.p: A grown-up loses about 2 to 3 litres of water a day. On a cool, quiet day, which of these lets water out without them noticing?
opts: Only urine
Breath and skin
Only tears
items.why: Breath and skin let water out all day without us noticing. Urine is a big part too, but we notice it. Tears are a tiny amount.

items.p: Kerala and Himachal Pradesh are very different places. Why do houses in both often have sloping roofs?
items.a: Kerala gets very heavy monsoon rain and Himachal gets snow. A sloping roof lets rain and snow slide off instead of sitting on top, where it could leak through or make the roof collapse.
items.why: A strong answer names what falls in each place and what the slope does to it.

items.p: Sort these by how long a person can live without them.
items.a: see items
items.why: The body stores almost no oxygen, a little water and quite a lot of energy as fat. The less of a need the body can store, the sooner it must be met.

items.p: Label where this body takes in its needs and where it lets things out: nose and mouth, skin, stomach, lungs.
items.a: Nose and mouth: air in, used air and water out. Lungs: oxygen in, carbon dioxide out. Stomach: food and drink in. Skin: water out all the time.
items.why: A strong answer shows the body taking in and giving out in several places at once.
items.art: An outline of a child's body with four blank label lines.

items.p: Some people say love is a basic need, like water. How could you find out whether a baby needs love as well as food?
items.a: A strong answer thinks about evidence: compare babies who get food and care with babies who get food but no one to hold them or talk to them. Doctors who have studied this found that babies without care often grow and learn less well, even with enough food.
items.why: This asks the child to think like a scientist about a big question. A strong answer says what to compare and what to look for, and notes that we must never harm a baby to find out.

items.p: Everyone needs exactly the same amount of water every day.
items.why: False. How much water a person needs depends on their size, the weather and how active they are. Food gives some water too. A child playing in the May sun needs more than a child sitting in a cool room.

items.p: Santorio called water that leaves the skin without us noticing insensible ____.
items.why: Perspiration means sweat. Insensible means we cannot sense it. Santorio named it in his book in 1614.

items.p: The water that leaves your skin today goes into the air. Where might it go after that?
items.a: It goes into the air as water vapour. Later it may cool and become part of a cloud, fall as rain, run into a lake or the ground, and be drunk by a plant, an animal or another person.
items.why: A strong answer follows the water out of the body and round the water cycle, back to another living thing.

applications: Doctors check for dehydration in children with fever or diarrhoea, and give ORS, a mix of water, salt and sugar.
Cities treat and pipe drinking water to homes so people do not fall ill.
Health workers run 'dry day' drives, asking families to empty still water once a week to stop dengue.
Architects put windows on two sides of rooms and exhaust fans in kitchens for ventilation.
Disaster teams pack water, dry food, sheets and clothes for families in cyclones and floods.
Sports coaches tell players to drink before and after a match, because a working body loses more water.
Clothes makers choose cotton for summer school uniforms and wool for winter wear.
Many families stand food cupboards or sugar dabbas in plates of water to keep ants out.

open_questions.q: How much water does each person really need to drink each day?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on size, weather, food and activity, and scientists still disagree about the best advice for healthy people.

open_questions.q: Is love or care a basic need in the same way as food and water?
open_questions.why_open: Babies without care often grow and learn less well, but people argue about how to compare needs of the body and needs of the mind.

open_questions.q: How will people keep enough safe drinking water as cities grow and the climate changes?
open_questions.why_open: Many Indian cities already run short of water in summer. Nobody yet knows the best mix of saving, storing and cleaning water for the future.

open_questions.q: Why do older people often feel less thirsty even when their body needs water?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know it happens, but not every reason for it is understood.

jokes.j: Why did the water bottle go to school?
jokes.a: To get a little more refreshed.

jokes.j: What did one lung say to the other?
jokes.a: Take a deep breath, I've got your back.

jokes.j: Why did the ant stop at the water ring?
What did the plate of idli say to the hungry child?
Why did the sweater stay in the cupboard in Chennai?
What do you call a house that is always out of breath?
Why was the mosquito sad on Sunday?
What did the hand say inside the plastic bag?
jokes.a: I'm not sweating it. Well, maybe a little.

jokes.j: Why did the crow sit by the water bowl?
jokes.a: She was waiting for her drinks order.

jokes.j: What is a cloud's favourite drink?
Why did the roof go to the doctor?
What did the cotton shirt say on a hot day?
jokes.a: Don't worry, I'll soak it up.

jokes.j: Why did the boy bring a ladder to the kitchen?

maths.problem: A child at rest breathes about 20 times a minute. How many breaths is that in 10 minutes? In one hour?
maths.answer: 200 breaths in 10 minutes, and 1,200 breaths in one hour.
maths.explain: 20 breaths each minute for 10 minutes is 20 times 10, which is 200. One hour is 60 minutes, so 20 times 60 is 1,200.
maths.context: This is about breathing. In the Hold and Wait activity you found you can't save up a breath.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how many breaths add up in a day, and why the body can never stop for long.

maths.problem: Santorio wrote that of 8 pounds of food and drink taken in a day, about 5 pounds leave the body unseen. Is that more or less than half? How do you know?
maths.explain: Half of 8 is 4. 5 is more than 4, so more than half leaves unseen. Only about 3 pounds leave in ways you can see.
maths.context: Santorio was a doctor in Italy who weighed himself, his food and his waste for about 30 years.
maths.why_maths: Comparing with half shows how big the unseen loss is: bigger than all the waste you can see.

maths.problem: Here are made-up results from a Water Ring test. Ants on the dry-plate sugar: 0 at the start, 3 after 30 minutes, 18 after 1 hour, 35 after 2 hours. Ants on the island sugar: 0 every time. Why did the number on the dry plate grow faster in the second half hour than in the first?
maths.answer: It grew by 3 in the first half hour and by 15 in the second. Once the first ants found the sugar, they laid a scent trail home, and many more ants followed it.
maths.explain: 18 minus 3 is 15, and 15 is 5 times as many as 3. A few scouts find food first. Then the trail brings the rest of the workers.
maths.context: This is about the Water Ring test, where one cap of sugar sat on a dry plate and one on an island in water.
maths.why_maths: Looking at how fast a number grows, not just how big it is, tells us how the ants were finding the food.

maths.problem: Kavya sat still with a bag on her hand, and saw mist after 6 minutes. Another day, she did 20 jumps first, and saw mist after 2 minutes. How many times faster did the mist come after jumping? Why?
maths.explain: 6 divided by 2 is 3. After jumping, her body was warmer and sweating to cool down, so more water left her skin.
maths.context: This is about the Hidden Water Test, where a plastic bag on a dry hand turns misty.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one time by the other gives one number that compares the two tests.

roots.context: We have found out what our bodies keep needing, and how families take care of those needs. Now we ask what our needs tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your hand felt dry, yet inside the bag it misted up within minutes. Your skin lets water out all the time, and so does every breath. Water you drank this morning is already leaving you. So you need water every day because your body never stops letting it go.
deep_truth.habit: We think of the body as a closed container, like a bottle that we fill and that then stays full. But a body is always open: water, used air and heat leave it every minute, so it must keep taking them in.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Hidden Water Test, the bag on a dry hand misted within minutes while the bag on an empty tumbler stayed clear. Santorio's weighing chair showed the same: more than half of what he ate and drank left him unseen.

three.who_am_i: You are a body that water and air keep passing through. Much of the water in you today was not in you a month ago.
three.what_is_life: A living being keeps taking in and giving out. An ant, a crow, a tulsi plant and you all need air and water every day.
three.what_is_this_world: The water that leaves your skin goes into the air, and may fall as rain somewhere else. Another living being will drink it.

roots.thread: Air goes in and out of you about 20 times a minute. Water leaves your skin, your breath and your body all day, and comes back in drinks and food. The same air and water pass through plants, ants, crows and people in turn. A tulsi plant gives out water from their leaves, and a crow drinks from a bowl. Our needs are the places where the world's air and water flow into us and out again.

science.text: In a grown-up, roughly a tenth of the water in the body is lost and replaced every day.
Plants give out oxygen in sunlight, and animals and people breathe it in. Animals and people give out carbon dioxide, and plants take it in.

other_view.view: The body has a clear boundary, the skin, and it works hard to keep its inside steady and different from the outside. Water passing through it is just chemistry. Calling it the world flowing through us is a way of speaking, not a new fact.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home in a city flat. The Hidden Water Test needs only see-through bags, a tumbler and loose hair bands. A dry hand mists a bag within about 5 to 10 minutes in a normal room, and drops form by 15 minutes, while the tumbler bag stays clear. In an AC room it can take 20 minutes, so the step says so. Bags are only ever for hands, and the band stays loose. The Water Ring test uses sugar in bottle caps near an ant path. Ants are found in nearly every Indian home, but they may take an hour or two, so the test is checked at 30 minutes and again at 1 to 2 hours, with an overnight fallback. A bridge such as a thread or crumb can let ants cross, so the steps check for one. No ants are harmed, and the trail is wiped at the end. The Breeze Path depends on some breeze, so it suggests the evening on a still day. Hold and Wait is done sitting down, never in water, and never as a contest. Nothing needs to be bought. The spine is the breath-holding start, the Hidden Water Test, the explanation cards, roots and the quiz, about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: Santorio Santorio was a doctor and a professor in Padua, in Italy. He wanted to measure the body, not only guess about it. So he hung a chair from a big balance and sat in it to eat his meals, watching the scale. For about thirty years he weighed himself, everything he ate and drank, and everything that came out of him as urine and stools. The numbers did not add up. The waste he could see weighed much less than the food and drink that went in, yet his own weight stayed about the same. So a large part must have been leaving his body where nobody could see it, through the skin and in the breath. In 1614 he published his results in a short book. He wrote that if a person takes in 8 pounds of food and drink in a day, about 5 pounds leave unseen. He called this insensible perspiration, meaning sweat that cannot be sensed. About 175 years later in Paris, Armand Seguin sat sealed in an airtight suit of varnished silk, breathing through a tube, while Antoine Lavoisier weighed him. They showed that both the skin and the breath carry water out.
how_we_found_out.who: Santorio Santorio, a doctor in Padua, Italy, and later Antoine Lavoisier and Armand Seguin in Paris
how_we_found_out.when: 1614 (Santorio's book Ars de statica medicina) and about 1790 (Lavoisier and Seguin)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many people think the body loses water only in ways they can see or feel: urine, and sweat on a hot day. Santorio's scale showed that more of what he ate and drank left him unseen than left as all his visible waste together.
